title: The psyche of Daniel Plainview from "There Will Be Blood"

commenti.body: [removed]

If you want a more literary analysis of what Daniel Plainview represents thematically:[this will do the trick](https://filmcolossus.com/there-will-be-blood-2007-explained)

I do believe that in a post-screening interview the host asked about Daniel’s background and DDL essentially said it wasn’t something he was all that concerned about. That at the end of the day the guy just liked to do the work. Which is one of the reasons he’s so miserable at the end. 

PTA jokes that they wanted to name the movie “You can take the man out of the mine, but you can’t take the mine out of the man” something like that.

They actually filmed a scene where Daniel was living in his tent in the mansion. But cut it because it felt a little too obvious.

"There are times when I look at people, and I see nothing worth liking. I want to earn enough money that I can get away from everyone."

I always thought he summed it up pretty well here.

I personally didn't think he was very complex. He was driven by money and greed, he disliked pretty much everybody, yet on the plus side he had bags of determination and perseverance. He did momentarily seem to feel bad about abandoning his son, and there were some scenes where it looked like he actually might have cared for him, but he only revealed the guilt for abandoning his son when he seemed to be backed into a corner, and he was quite happy to send him away so that he could focus on moneymaking. Towards the end when he's living in his mansion and his son goes to see him, you can clearly see that Daniel's level of self-centredness trumps any goodwill he has for his son's business venture. He certainly had sociopathic tendencies.

On the acting side, Daniel Day Lewis gives a wholy memorable performance. Daniel Plainview is a character that I would put in the category of larger in the life film characters, such as Tony Montana.

But then he sort of subtly contradicts that with "I have a competition in me. I want no one else to succeed". Does he want to get away from everyone or does he want to crush them? Does he want to get away from everyone BECAUSE of his overwhelming desire to crush them? Or is it all just bravado disguising very probable abandonment issues?

Lol. He's not complex at all. He's a white colonizer who sees everything as an object. Oil is an object, religion is an object, people are objects. The story might be compelling, but Daniel Plainview is just another uninteresting white boy.
Oil is literally an object.

One could interpret Daniel Plainview as a purely evil character, but in the scene on the train where he's (iirc) separating from HW, you can see him shed a single tear. That tiny detail alone completely changes the relationship between Daniel and HW. 

Despite their falling out at the end of the movie, Daniel Plainview did have genuine affection for HW and didn't just see him as a tool.

A lifetime of actions speak infinitely louder than a single tear.

He had that brief moment of guilt or remorse or whatever it was... but then went right back to focusing on nothing but himself
Weird you find race to be significant. IIRC everyone he victimized was also white

He’s very conflicted. He wants to connect with people (his fake brother, his adopted child) but his greed and his paranoia and his hatred push him away from people. That’s the conflict at the heart of the movie.

I don't know if I agree that it's the heart, but it's there. To me the moments of connection or attempts at connection are just insights into what else might be going on in his head, but if there ever was a conflict, the greed has long won by the time we meet him.
I mean taking in and raising a child is a sign of him trying to care for other people. But eventually his greed and resentment pushes him away at the end.

On one level, he's the rapacious spirit of capitalism

I do enjoy his visceral distaste for Eli's religion and, seemingly, religion in general. Like the scene where he displays his dominance over Eli's dad by telling the daughter she won't get beaten any more (or however that scene goes). Or, obviously, their three slapstick physical altercations

Sure, you can interpret it as an outgrowth of his need for total dominance and control. But it really does seem to go beyond that into a more personal, idiosyncratic animus. He dislikes religion more than he needs to, I think

But even at the time of him taking in H.W., he's deep into his one-track-minded pursuit of riches. I've always been of the mind that he knows what's right and wrong, but resents that these principles exist in the world, because he doesn't actually believe them. But he can use his understanding of these principles to succeed, and being able to present himself as a family man could be beneficial to him. He doesn't just want to get away from people, he hates people.
Thanks for sharing this article!
Thanks for reading

I’ve always taken him as someone who has been hurt in his past in a way we don’t exactly know how. Maybe growing up in grueling poverty with abusive parents. But he basically comes to the audience as someone with lots of psychic scares. I don’t view him as a psychopath that doesn’t like that he has emotions. I’ve viewed him as a very traumatized person who thinks that people will only disappoint and betray you because that was what he has dealt with in his past.

He’s a man who hates himself and projects it onto the world. If you pay attention to that movie, everyone is pretty nice to Daniel other than maybe the other oil businessmen. It doesn’t really make sense that he seems to hate people who are nothing but kind or minding their own business. He feels lonely because he’s chosen to isolate himself in misery and ambition

I think this oversimplifies him. Yeah I mean that’s a one-sentence summary of him, but he also tries to form bonds with people. He’s uncomfortable with it, and it’s not natural, but it’s something that he tries to do at various times. Adopting a kid, taking in a “brother,” even smaller things like protecting the girl his son likes. 

But at the end of the day, it’s not natural for him and he’s not good at it. And — given there’s a competition in him — when he fails at forming bonds and making friends, he lashes out and pulls away. There’s a lot of self-loathing as a result, as we can see with his drinking getting worse and worse over time, and this internal competition steadily sides with the part of him that’s just out to win and conquer and make more money. By the end, he’s a completely broken, hateful person without any morals left. And that’s what does him in.

Of course!  It’s one of the movies I’ve seen which I feel is pure perfection but I never desire to see again because it’s so painful!  I loved reading the analysis and agree with almost everything.

I think his dislike of religion is just a byproduct of his total one-minded devotion to capitalism. When Daniel looks at the world around him, he sees a sick world that is plagued by one thing: people. He wants to escape the world and people which is pretty much the exact opposite of religion where you need to be connected to others for your life to have meaning.  When Daniel tries to cut off his son, Eli forcefully drags him back out into the open at the Baptism. But, ultimately, religion is just one more thing for Daniel to escape through money, and Eli is getting in the way of his making more money and achieving that goal, so I don't think he hates religion more than any other thing that groups of people do haha. And I think the juxtaposition between religion and capitalism is imposed more by the filmmakers than Daniels mind.

I have to agree with this article...

He's clearly a monster, but there's these shreds of longing buried deep inside him at certain moments. There's moments of longing for HW. And there's a brief moment of longing for his fake brother. Yes, these are utterly overshadowed by his growing greed and hatred of people, but there's enough there to make one see the other side. 

I'm not trying to say he's likeable or made likeable. Just that there's a shred of longing there. As the essay points out, the last two scenes put that longing to rest. HW becomes a competitor, and so Daniel tells him the truth and disowns him, strips himself of whatever shred of longing may have been lingering after all those decades. Then he's free to murder and devour Eli, which he secretly had wished for all those years.
